claim: Reverberation produces many delayed and distorted copies of the original sound.
source: In almost every natural environment, sounds are reflected by nearby objects, producing many delayed and distorted copies of the original sound, known as reverberation.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about reverberation that draws from established scientific understanding of acoustics.

claim: The auditory system usually copes well with reverberation, allowing recognition of sound sources regardless of their environments.
source: Our brains usually cope well with reverberation, allowing us to recognize sound sources regardless of their environments.
evidence: This statement is supported by general scientific knowledge about auditory perception.

claim: Reverberation can cause severe difficulties for speech recognition algorithms and hearing-impaired people.
source: In contrast, reverberation can cause severe difficulties for speech recognition algorithms and hearing-impaired people.
evidence: This is supported by citations provided later in the manuscript about these difficulties.

claim: A linear model was trained to recover natural, anechoic sounds from their simulated reverberant counterparts.
source: We trained a linear model to recover a rich set of natural, anechoic sounds from their simulated reverberant counterparts.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The model neurons achieved dereverberation by extending the inhibitory component of their receptive filters for more reverberant spaces.
source: The model neurons achieved this by extending the inhibitory component of their receptive filters for more reverberant spaces, and did so in a frequency-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model described in the study.

claim: The model neurons extended inhibitory components in a frequency-dependent manner.
source: The model neurons achieved this by extending the inhibitory component of their receptive filters for more reverberant spaces, and did so in a frequency-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational model.

claim: The predicted effects from the model were observed in the responses of auditory cortical neurons of ferrets in simulated reverberant environments.
source: These predicted effects were observed in the responses of auditory cortical neurons of ferrets in the same simulated reverberant environments.
evidence: This describes the experimental validation of model predictions.

claim: Auditory cortical neurons adapt to reverberation by adjusting their filtering properties in a manner consistent with dereverberation.
source: Together, these results suggest that auditory cortical neurons adapt to reverberation by adjusting their filtering properties in a manner consistent with dereverberation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined model and experimental results.

claim: Sound reflections are attenuated and distorted due to frequency-selective absorption.
source: Compared to the original sound, these reflections are attenuated and distorted due to frequency-selective absorption and delayed due to increased path length (Kuttruff, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuttruff, 2017.

claim: Sound reflections are delayed due to increased path length.
source: Compared to the original sound, these reflections are attenuated and distorted due to frequency-selective absorption and delayed due to increased path length (Kuttruff, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuttruff, 2017.

claim: Reverberation can help judge room size, sound-source distance, and realism.
source: Reverberation can be useful, helping us judge room size, sound-source distance, and realism (Shinn-Cunningham, 2000; Trivedi et al., 2009; Kolarik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Strong reverberation can impair sound-source localization.
source: However, strong reverberation can impair sound-source localization (Hartmann, 1982; Shinn-Cunningham and Kawakyu, 2003; Rakerd and Hartmann, 2005; Shinn-Cunningham et al., 2005) and segregation (Culling et al., 1994; Darwin and Hukin, 2000), pitch discrimination (Sayles and Winter, 2008), and speech recognition (Knudsen, 1929; Nábĕlek et al., 1989; Guediche et al., 2014; Houtgast and Steeneken, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Strong reverberation can impair sound segregation.
source: However, strong reverberation can impair sound-source localization (Hartmann, 1982; Shinn-Cunningham and Kawakyu, 2003; Rakerd and Hartmann, 2005; Shinn-Cunningham et al., 2005) and segregation (Culling et al., 1994; Darwin and Hukin, 2000), pitch discrimination (Sayles and Winter, 2008), and speech recognition (Knudsen, 1929; Nábĕlek et al., 1989; Guediche et al., 2014; Houtgast and Steeneken, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Strong reverberation can impair pitch discrimination.
source: However, strong reverberation can impair sound-source localization (Hartmann, 1982; Shinn-Cunningham and Kawakyu, 2003; Rakerd and Hartmann, 2005; Shinn-Cunningham et al., 2005) and segregation (Culling et al., 1994; Darwin and Hukin, 2000), pitch discrimination (Sayles and Winter, 2008), and speech recognition (Knudsen, 1929; Nábĕlek et al., 1989; Guediche et al., 2014; Houtgast and Steeneken, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sayles and Winter, 2008.

claim: Strong reverberation can impair speech recognition.
source: However, strong reverberation can impair sound-source localization (Hartmann, 1982; Shinn-Cunningham and Kawakyu, 2003; Rakerd and Hartmann, 2005; Shinn-Cunningham et al., 2005) and segregation (Culling et al., 1994; Darwin and Hukin, 2000), pitch discrimination (Sayles and Winter, 2008), and speech recognition (Knudsen, 1929; Nábĕlek et al., 1989; Guediche et al., 2014; Houtgast and Steeneken, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Reverberation can be detrimental for people with hearing impairments, increasing tone detection thresholds.
source: Notably, reverberation can be detrimental for people with hearing impairments, increasing tone detection thresholds and reducing intelligibility of consonants (Humes et al., 1986; Helfer and Wilber, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Humes et al., 1986 and Helfer and Wilber, 1990.

claim: Reverberation reduces intelligibility of consonants for people with hearing impairments.
source: Notably, reverberation can be detrimental for people with hearing impairments, increasing tone detection thresholds and reducing intelligibility of consonants (Humes et al., 1986; Helfer and Wilber, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Humes et al., 1986 and Helfer and Wilber, 1990.

claim: Reverberation can impede the effectiveness of hearing aids.
source: It can also impede the effectiveness of auditory prostheses such as hearing aids (Qin and Oxenham, 2005; Poissant et al., 2006) and substantially reduces the performance of automatic speech recognition devices (Yoshioka et al., 2012; Kinoshita et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Qin and Oxenham, 2005 and Poissant et al., 2006.

claim: Reverberation substantially reduces the performance of automatic speech recognition devices.
source: It can also impede the effectiveness of auditory prostheses such as hearing aids (Qin and Oxenham, 2005; Poissant et al., 2006) and substantially reduces the performance of automatic speech recognition devices (Yoshioka et al., 2012; Kinoshita et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoshioka et al., 2012 and Kinoshita et al., 2016.

claim: Healthy listeners often only directly notice reverberation when it is strong.
source: The auditory system has mechanisms to help us cope with reverberation, to the extent that healthy listeners often only directly notice it when it is strong (in environments such as cathedrals).
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about auditory perception.

claim: Healthy listeners can perform sound localization in the presence of mild-to-moderate reverberation.
source: In the presence of mild-to-moderate reverberation, healthy listeners can continue to perform sound localization (Hartmann, 1982; Rakerd and Hartmann, 2005) and speech and auditory object recognition tasks (Houtgast and Steeneken, 1985; Bradley, 1986; Darwin and Hukin, 2000; Culling et al., 2003; Nielsen and Dau, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hartmann, 1982 and Rakerd and Hartmann, 2005.

claim: Healthy listeners can perform speech and auditory object recognition tasks in the presence of mild-to-moderate reverberation.
source: In the presence of mild-to-moderate reverberation, healthy listeners can continue to perform sound localization (Hartmann, 1982; Rakerd and Hartmann, 2005) and speech and auditory object recognition tasks (Houtgast and Steeneken, 1985; Bradley, 1986; Darwin and Hukin, 2000; Culling et al., 2003; Nielsen and Dau, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous studies have examined subcortical processes that facilitate localization of reverberant sounds.
source: Previous studies have examined subcortical processes that facilitate localization of reverberant sounds (Yin, 1994; Litovsky and Yin, 1998; Fitzpatrick et al., 1999; Spitzer et al., 2004; Tollin et al., 2004; Pecka et al., 2007; Devore et al., 2009; Kuwada et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2015; Brughera et al., 2021), and how subcortical processing of synthetic periodic sounds is disrupted by reverberation (Sayles and Winter, 2008) and partially restored by compensatory mechanisms (Slama and Delgutte, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Subcortical processing of synthetic periodic sounds is disrupted by reverberation.
source: Previous studies have examined subcortical processes that facilitate localization of reverberant sounds (Yin, 1994; Litovsky and Yin, 1998; Fitzpatrick et al., 1999; Spitzer et al., 2004; Tollin et al., 2004; Pecka et al., 2007; Devore et al., 2009; Kuwada et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2015; Brughera et al., 2021), and how subcortical processing of synthetic periodic sounds is disrupted by reverberation (Sayles and Winter, 2008) and partially restored by compensatory mechanisms (Slama and Delgutte, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sayles and Winter, 2008.

claim: Subcortical processing of synthetic periodic sounds is partially restored by compensatory mechanisms after reverberation disruption.
source: Previous studies have examined subcortical processes that facilitate localization of reverberant sounds (Yin, 1994; Litovsky and Yin, 1998; Fitzpatrick et al., 1999; Spitzer et al., 2004; Tollin et al., 2004; Pecka et al., 2007; Devore et al., 2009; Kuwada et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2015; Brughera et al., 2021), and how subcortical processing of synthetic periodic sounds is disrupted by reverberation (Sayles and Winter, 2008) and partially restored by compensatory mechanisms (Slama and Delgutte, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Slama and Delgutte, 2015.

claim: Much less is known about the neural processing of speech and other complex natural sounds in the presence of reverberation.
source: Much less is known about the neural processing of speech and other complex natural sounds in the presence of reverberation.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Representations of sounds that are invariant to non-reverberant background noise emerge at the level of auditory cortex via neuronal adaptation to stimulus statistics.
source: However, converging evidence from electrophysiological recordings in animals (Rabinowitz et al., 2013; Moore et al., 2013; Mesgarani et al., 2014) and from human EEG (Khalighinejad et al., 2019) and fMRI (Kell and McDermott, 2019) studies suggests that representations of sounds that are invariant to non-reverberant background noise emerge at the level of auditory cortex via neuronal adaptation to stimulus statistics (but see also Lohse et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to animal and human studies.

claim: Auditory cortex may play a similar role in adaptation to reverberation as it does for non-reverberant background noise.
source: Auditory cortex may play a similar role in adaptation to reverberation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous findings about noise adaptation.

claim: Speech and vocalization stimuli reconstructed from auditory cortical responses in awake ferrets more closely resemble their anechoic versions than the reverberant ones, even if the sounds were presented in reverberant environments.
source: Indeed, speech and vocalization stimuli reconstructed from auditory cortical responses in awake ferrets more closely resemble their anechoic versions than the reverberant ones, even if the sounds were presented in reverberant environments (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mesgarani et al., 2014.

claim: Similar results to ferret studies have been found in humans using sound reconstructions from EEG measurements.
source: Similar results have been found in humans using sound reconstructions from EEG measurements (Fuglsang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fuglsang et al., 2017.

claim: It remains unclear whether the observed cortical invariance to reverberation can occur in the absence of top-down attention.
source: It remains unclear, however, whether the observed cortical invariance to reverberation can occur in the absence of top-down attention, and through what neural mechanisms this is achieved.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: It remains unclear through what neural mechanisms cortical invariance to reverberation is achieved.
source: It remains unclear, however, whether the observed cortical invariance to reverberation can occur in the absence of top-down attention, and through what neural mechanisms this is achieved.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The study used a model to predict what neural tuning properties would be useful for effective attenuation of reverberation.
source: Here, we addressed these questions by using a model to predict what neural tuning properties would be useful for effective attenuation of reverberation (a normative 'dereverberation model').
evidence: This describes the methodology of the study.

claim: The study tested model predictions using neural recordings in the auditory cortex of anesthetized ferrets.
source: We then test these predictions using neural recordings in the auditory cortex of anesthetized ferrets.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: The study made reverberant versions of natural sounds in simulated rooms of different sizes.
source: More specifically, we made reverberant versions of natural sounds in simulated rooms of different sizes.
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation method.

claim: A linear model was trained to retrieve the clean anechoic sounds from their reverberant versions.
source: Next, we trained a linear model to retrieve the clean anechoic sounds from their reverberant versions.
evidence: This describes the model training procedure.

claim: With increased reverberation, neurons should adapt so that they are inhibited by sound energy further into the past.
source: Our trained model provided specific predictions for how the brain may achieve this task: with increased reverberation, neurons should adapt so that they are inhibited by sound energy further into the past, and this should occur in a sound frequency-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: The inhibitory adaptation to reverberation should occur in a sound frequency-dependent manner.
source: Our trained model provided specific predictions for how the brain may achieve this task: with increased reverberation, neurons should adapt so that they are inhibited by sound energy further into the past, and this should occur in a sound frequency-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a prediction from the computational model.

claim: The predicted effects were observed in the responses of auditory cortical neurons to natural sounds presented in simulated reverberant rooms.
source: We observed these predicted effects in the responses of auditory cortical neurons to natural sounds presented in simulated reverberant rooms, and show that they arise from an adaptive process.
evidence: This describes the experimental findings.

claim: The observed effects arise from an adaptive process.
source: We observed these predicted effects in the responses of auditory cortical neurons to natural sounds presented in simulated reverberant rooms, and show that they arise from an adaptive process.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Auditory cortical neurons may support hearing performance in reverberant spaces by temporally extending the inhibitory component of their spectrotemporal receptive fields.
source: These results suggest that auditory cortical neurons may support hearing performance in reverberant spaces by temporally extending the inhibitory component of their spectrotemporal receptive fields.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: For each room, on a held-out test set, the dereverberation model reduced the difference between the incoming reverberant cochleagram and the anechoic cochleagram by 26% for the small room.
source: For each room, on a held-out test set, the dereverberation model reduced the difference between the incoming reverberant cochleagram and the anechoic cochleagram (small room mean squared error reduction 26%; large room reduction 20%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation.

claim: For each room, on a held-out test set, the dereverberation model reduced the difference between the incoming reverberant cochleagram and the anechoic cochleagram by 20% for the large room.
source: For each room, on a held-out test set, the dereverberation model reduced the difference between the incoming reverberant cochleagram and the anechoic cochleagram (small room mean squared error reduction 26%; large room reduction 20%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model evaluation.

claim: The majority of the excitatory and inhibitory weights in model kernels appear localized around a particular frequency, resembling the frequency tuning seen in auditory cortical neurons.
source: The majority of the excitatory and inhibitory weights appear localized around a particular frequency, resembling the frequency tuning seen in auditory cortical neurons (Bizley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an observation from the model results, supported by a citation to Bizley et al., 2005.

claim: The model kernels had temporally asymmetric structure, where strongest excitatory weights tended to occur first, followed soon after by a longer inhibitory field.
source: The model kernels had temporally asymmetric structure, where strongest excitatory weights tended to occur first (Figure 2A), followed soon after by a longer inhibitory field.
evidence: This is an observation from the model results, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: The pattern of temporally asymmetric structure with early excitation followed by inhibition has been commonly observed in the spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) of auditory cortical neurons.
source: This pattern has been commonly observed in the spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) of auditory cortical neurons (deCharms et al., 1998; Linden et al., 2003; Harper et al., 2016; Rahman et al., 2019), so our model qualitatively reproduces the basic frequency tuning and temporal characteristics of auditory cortical neurons.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The inhibitory components of the large-room kernels tended to be delayed and longer in duration, relative to the small-room kernels.
source: Importantly, we can compare the model kernels for the large room with those for the small room. The inhibitory components of the large-room kernels tended to be delayed and longer in duration, relative to the small-room kernels (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from the model results, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: The temporal profile of the excitatory components was similar for the small and large rooms in the model kernels.
source: In contrast, the temporal profile of the excitatory components was similar for the small and large rooms.
evidence: This is an observation from the model results.

claim: 2244 auditory cortical units were recorded.
source: We recorded the responses of 2244 auditory cortical units.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: 696 units (160 single units, 23%) were responsive to the stimuli and used for further analysis.
source: Of these, the 696 units (160 single units, 23%) that were responsive to the stimuli were used for further analysis (see Spike sorting).
evidence: This is a description of the data selection criteria.

claim: The model kernels show similarity to the STRFs typically reported for auditory cortical neurons.
source: As mentioned above, the model kernels show some similarity to the STRFs typically reported for auditory cortical neurons (deCharms et al., 1998; Linden et al., 2003; Harper et al., 2016; Rahman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison between model and known neurophysiological data, supported by citations.

claim: The model kernels show similarity to the STRFs measured in the current study, including having frequency tuning, early excitatory receptive fields and delayed inhibitory receptive fields.
source: Likewise, the model kernels show similarity to the STRFs we present here, including having frequency tuning, early excitatory receptive fields and delayed inhibitory receptive fields (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a comparison between model and experimental results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: 266 cortical units were recorded from 2 ferrets for the extended stimulus set with three room sizes.
source: We measured auditory cortical responses to this extended stimulus set in 2 ferrets (266 cortical units).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: As room size, and hence reverberation time, was increased, there was an increase in the delay of inhibition in the tuning properties of auditory cortical neurons.
source: Thus, as room size, and hence reverberation time, was increased, we observed an increase in the delay of inhibition in the tuning properties of auditory cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The increase in inhibition delay is consistent with a normative model of dereverberation.
source: This increase is consistent with a normative model of dereverberation, suggesting that the tuning properties of auditory cortical neurons may adapt in order to dereverberate incoming sounds.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of the model.

claim: Differences in sound statistics between the reverberation conditions could result in different STRFs, even if the underlying neuronal tuning is unchanged.
source: An important possibility is that differences in sound statistics between the reverberation conditions could result in different STRFs, even if the underlying neuronal tuning is unchanged.
evidence: This is a potential confound that the authors consider.

claim: The cochleagrams of more reverberant sounds are more temporally blurred.
source: For example, the cochleagrams of more reverberant sounds are more temporally blurred (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the stimulus representations, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Temporal blurring in cochleagrams could lead to slower features in the neuronal STRFs for the larger room, purely due to systematic model fitting artefacts.
source: This could lead to slower features in the neuronal STRFs for the larger room, purely due to systematic model fitting artefacts (Christianson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a potential confound, supported by a citation to Christianson et al., 2008.

claim: For each recorded cortical unit, a simulated linear-nonlinear (LN) model neuron was fitted, composed of a single STRF feeding into a non-linear output function.
source: As a first test, for each recorded cortical unit, we fitted a simulated linear-nonlinear (LN) model neuron (Schwartz et al., 2006), composed of a single STRF (fitted to the combined small and large room stimuli) feeding into a non-linear output function (see Simulated neurons).
evidence: This describes the control analysis methodology.

claim: The noise in the recorded neuronal responses was close to Poisson (median Fano factor = 1.1).
source: The noise in the recorded neuronal responses was close to Poisson (median Fano factor = 1.1).
evidence: This is a characterization of the neuronal response variability.

claim: Differences in stimulus properties alone can account for a small shift in inhibitory receptive fields across rooms, but not the magnitude of delay observed in neural data.
source: In summary, these simulations suggest that differences in stimulus properties alone can account for a small shift in inhibitory receptive fields across rooms, but not the magnitude of delay that we observed in our neural data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control simulation analysis.

claim: The observed effects are likely to arise, at least in part, from neural adaptation to room reverberation.
source: Therefore, these effects are likely to arise, at least in part, from neural adaptation to room reverberation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control simulation analysis.

claim: The NRFP model could not explain the magnitude of the shift in inhibitory center of mass or peak time seen in the real data.
source: As with the LNP model, the NRFP model could not explain the magnitude of the shift in inhibitory center of mass or peak time seen in the real data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the control simulation analysis with the NRFP model.

claim: An increased non-linearity alone cannot account for the reverberation adaptation observed in auditory cortex.
source: This suggests that an increased non-linearity alone cannot account for the reverberation adaptation observed in auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the NRFP model analysis.

claim: The neuronal responses to the noise probe showed a similar initial onset excitation (5–25ms) in both conditions.
source: The neuronal responses to the noise probe showed a similar initial onset excitation (5–25ms) in both conditions, but the return to baseline firing was slower in the large room condition (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the noise probe analysis.

claim: The return to baseline firing after the noise probe was slower in the large room condition.
source: The neuronal responses to the noise probe showed a similar initial onset excitation (5–25ms) in both conditions, but the return to baseline firing was slower in the large room condition (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the noise probe analysis.

claim: Responses to an anechoic probe noise show further evidence for reverberation adaptation in auditory cortical neurons.
source: Therefore, responses to an anechoic probe noise show further evidence for reverberation adaptation in auditory cortical neurons, and are consistent with the predicted delayed inhibition in the presence of increased reverberation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the noise probe analysis.

claim: The switching stimulus was tested in 310 cortical units across 4 ferrets.
source: This switching stimulus was tested in 310 cortical units across 4 ferrets.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: The switching stimulus results further suggest that auditory cortical receptive fields are genuinely adapting dynamically to the changing reverberant conditions.
source: These results further suggest that auditory cortical receptive fields are genuinely adapting dynamically to the changing reverberant conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the switching stimulus analysis.

claim: 430 cortical units were recorded from 5 ferrets for the reverberation invariance analysis.
source: We did this for 430 cortical units recorded from 5 ferrets, and included an anechoic room condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data collected.

claim: The real neural responses showed significantly larger correlation coefficients between reverberation conditions than did the simulated neural responses for all three pairs of reverberant conditions (p<0.0001).
source: In all three cases, the real neural responses showed significantly larger correlation coefficients between reverberation conditions than did the simulated neural responses (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; p<0.0001; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the reverberation invariance analysis.

claim: The adaptation observed plays a role in dereverberation by producing neural representations of sounds that are similar across reverberant conditions.
source: These results suggest that the adaptation we observed plays a role in dereverberation by producing neural representations of sounds that are similar across reverberant conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the reverberation invariance analysis.

claim: In both the model and the neuronal data, while the temporal spread of the excitatory components stays relatively constant across the preferred frequency, the inhibitory components tend to extend less far back in time as the preferred frequency increases.
source: A visual inspection of these plots reveals that in both the model and the neuronal data, while the temporal spread of the excitatory components stays relatively constant across the preferred frequency, the inhibitory components tend to extend less far back in time as the preferred frequency increases.
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency-dependent analysis.

claim: The inhibitory components occurred systematically later in model kernels that were tuned to lower frequencies, in both the small (r = –0.57, p = 0.0037) and large room (r = –0.80, p = 2.6 × 10-6) simulations.
source: The inhibitory components occurred systematically later in model kernels that were tuned to lower frequencies, in both the small (Pearson's correlation: r = –0.57, p = 0.0037) and large room (r = –0.80, p = 2.6 × 10-6) simulations.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the frequency-dependent analysis of model kernels.

claim: The inhibitory components were later in time in the large room than in the small room across the entire best frequency range, for both the dereverberation model and neuronal data.
source: Figure 7A and B also show that the inhibitory components were later in time in the large room than in the small room across the entire best frequency range, for both the dereverberation model and neuronal data.
evidence: This is an observation from the frequency-dependent analysis.

claim: The dereverberation model recapitulated known properties of auditory cortical neurons, such as frequency tuning and temporally asymmetric STRFs with excitation followed by inhibition.
source: We confirmed the validity of our dereverberation model by showing that it recapitulated known properties of auditory cortical neurons, such as frequency tuning and temporally asymmetric STRFs with excitation followed by inhibition (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a validation of the model against known neurophysiological properties.

claim: The dereverberation model makes two novel predictions: (1) the inhibitory components of neuronal STRFs should be more delayed in more reverberant conditions; and (2) the inhibition should occur earlier for higher sound frequencies.
source: Interestingly, our dereverberation model also makes two novel predictions: (1) the inhibitory components of neuronal STRFs should be more delayed in more reverberant conditions (Figure 3); and (2) the inhibition should occur earlier for higher sound frequencies (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2 , Figure 7).
evidence: These are predictions from the computational model.

claim: Both predictions from the dereverberation model were verified using electrophysiological recordings from ferret auditory cortex neurons.
source: We verified both of these predictions using electrophysiological recordings from ferret auditory cortex neurons, fitting STRFs to neuronal responses to sounds from the same rich dataset, and comparing them to the model kernels.
evidence: This describes the experimental validation of model predictions.

claim: The observed changes in the neuronal STRFs are consistent with a truly adaptive dynamic process.
source: Finally, we used three additional methods – non-adaptive simulated neurons, probe stimuli and switching stimuli – to confirm that the observed changes in the neuronal STRFs are consistent with a truly adaptive dynamic process (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion from multiple control analyses.

claim: The population of auditory cortex neurons adapt to reverberation by extending their inhibitory field in time in a frequency-dependent manner.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the population of auditory cortex neurons adapt to reverberation by extending their inhibitory field in time in a frequency-dependent manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Human hearing is remarkably robust to reverberation when listeners discriminate speech and naturalistic sounds.
source: Previous studies have shown that human hearing is remarkably robust to reverberation when listeners discriminate speech and naturalistic sounds (Houtgast and Steeneken, 1985; Bradley, 1986; Darwin and Hukin, 2000; Culling et al., 2003; Nielsen and Dau, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The neurophysiological results in the ferret auditory cortex are consistent with robust representation of sounds in reverberation.
source: Our neurophysiological results in the ferret auditory cortex are consistent with such robust representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of previous findings.

claim: Neurons recorded in the auditory cortex tend to adapt their responses in a way that is consistent with the computational goal of removing reverberation from natural sounds, even in anesthetized animals.
source: We find that neurons recorded in the auditory cortex tend to adapt their responses in a way that is consistent with the computational goal of removing reverberation from natural sounds, even in anesthetized animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The results are in good agreement with a previous study in awake passive listening ferrets, which showed that anechoic speech and vocalizations were more readily decodable from the responses of auditory cortex neurons to echoic sounds than the echoic sounds themselves.
source: Our results are also in good agreement with a previous study in awake passive listening ferrets, which showed that anechoic speech and vocalizations were more readily decodable from the responses of auditory cortex neurons to echoic sounds than the echoic sounds themselves (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous findings, supported by a citation.

claim: A similar study in humans using EEG corroborated findings that speech envelopes reconstructed from neural responses to reverberated stimuli resembled the original anechoic stimuli more than the echoic input, but only when listeners attended to the sound sources.
source: A similar study in humans using EEG corroborated these findings, showing speech envelopes reconstructed from neural responses to the reverberated stimuli resembled the original anechoic stimuli more than the echoic input, but only when listeners attended to the sound sources (Fuglsang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fuglsang et al., 2017.

claim: A human MEG study suggests that auditory cortex may contain both reverberant and dereverberated representations of speech in reverberant conditions.
source: Interestingly, a human MEG study suggests that auditory cortex may contain both reverberant and dereverberated representations of speech in reverberant conditions (Puvvada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Puvvada et al., 2017.

claim: Traer and McDermott, 2016 found that humans were able to discriminate different reverberant conditions well with both familiar and unfamiliar sounds.
source: In addition, Traer and McDermott, 2016 found that humans were able to discriminate different reverberant conditions well with both familiar and unfamiliar sounds.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Traer and McDermott, 2016.

claim: Although most cortical neurons adapted to reverberation, it is possible that some of them might carry information about the reverberant environment or even represent it more explicitly.
source: Thus, although most cortical neurons adapted to reverberation, it is possible that some of them might carry information about the reverberant environment or even represent it more explicitly.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation of heterogeneous responses.

claim: The larger variance in reverberation adaptation across neural units may result from the fact that neural responses are inherently noisier than model kernels.
